channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: SOGC Clinical Practice Guideline No. 471: Alcohol and Pregnancy.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a national clinical practice guideline (GRADE method) from the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) updating standards for screening, brief intervention, and referral for alcohol use in pregnant women and women of childbearing age. It synthesises evidence from 2018–2026 across Medline, EMBASE and CENTRAL to inform obstetric and primary care providers.
FINDINGS: The guideline recommends universal screening for alcohol use with validated tools (e.g., AUDIT-C) and brief interventions for all pregnant women and women planning pregnancy. It advises expedited referral pathways to alcohol cessation services and prioritised access to specialist support. Evidence quality was graded using GRADE, with most recommendations rated as moderate to low certainty due to heterogeneity in study designs and populations.
INTERPRETATION: As a guideline, internal validity is high in terms of methodological rigour (GRADE framework, systematic search), but external validity depends on local healthcare system capacity for referral and follow-up. The strength of recommendations is tempered by the low-to-moderate quality of underlying evidence, particularly for pharmacological interventions during pregnancy. The document does not quantify effect sizes or absolute risk reductions, so clinical significance remains inferred rather than empirically demonstrated.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should adopt routine screening and brief interventions for alcohol use in pregnancy and preconception care, ensuring clear referral pathways to addiction services. The lack of robust effect estimates means centres should monitor local outcomes when implementing these recommendations.

item.title: The effects of virtual reality interventions on outcomes related to well-being among autistic children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether virtual reality (VR) interventions improve subjective well-being (SWB) or psychological well-being (PWB) in autistic children, using randomized controlled trials (RCTs) synthesized in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
FINDINGS: VR showed a positive but nonsignificant effect on SWB-related outcomes (g = 0.37, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.78], p = 0.07), while a statistically significant positive effect was found for PWB-related outcomes (g = 0.45, 95% CI [0.27, 0.63], p < 0.05). The meta-analysis included 10 RCTs, with 70% raising some risk-of-bias concerns and only eight effect sizes contributing to the PWB estimate.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the PWB result is limited by risk-of-bias concerns, small numbers of contributing studies, and heterogeneity in interventions and outcomes. The SWB finding is not statistically significant, so no firm conclusions can be drawn. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized outcome measures are needed before VR can be recommended for routine use.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests potential benefit of VR for psychological well-being in autistic children within research settings, but not yet for routine clinical practice; clinicians should await more robust trials before adopting VR for well-being outcomes.

item.title: Skin and Brain in Bipolar Disorder: A Review of Dermatologic-Psychotropic Drug Interactions.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines bidirectional dermatologic–psychotropic drug interactions in patients with bipolar disorder, focusing on how systemic dermatologic medications may destabilise mood and how mood stabilisers/antipsychotics may provoke clinically important cutaneous adverse reactions. It synthesises case reports, observational studies and pharmacovigilance data indexed to June 2026, but no randomised trials were identified.
FINDINGS: Dermatologic agents such as isotretinoin, systemic corticosteroids and methotrexate have been linked to mood destabilisation in susceptible individuals. Conversely, lithium and lamotrigine carry dermatologic risks including acneiform or psoriasiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa and severe cutaneous adverse reactions. No quantitative effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is entirely observational and heterogeneous (case reports, series, pharmacovigilance), so causality cannot be established and effect sizes remain unknown. Strengths include broad coverage of drug pairs and explicit acknowledgment of gaps. Limitations include lack of controlled data, potential publication bias and unclear generalisability beyond bipolar populations. Clinically meaningful magnitudes of risk cannot be quantified from this review.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until better evidence emerges, clinicians should screen for prior psychiatric episodes and cutaneous drug reactions, counsel patients about possible bidirectional risks, and monitor closely when initiating or escalating high-risk therapies; shared decision-making across specialties is advised.

item.title: Prevalence of mental health outcomes among trans and gender diverse adults: a global systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This global systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised 207 studies (n=134 071) to estimate current/lifetime prevalence of depression, anxiety, PTSD, suicidality and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) among trans and gender-diverse adults, addressing gaps in prior reviews that often focused on youth or selected samples.
FINDINGS: Pooled prevalence estimates were 40.1 % (95 % CI 35.6–44.8) for depression, 29.8 % (20.3–40.2) for anxiety and 23.6 % (14.9–33.5) for PTSD. Past-12-month rates were 43.1 % (38.9–47.3) for suicidal ideation, 9.3 % (7.7–11.0) for suicide attempts and 26.1 % (20.4–32.2) for NSSI. Non-binary participants appeared to have higher rates, and estimates varied by assessment method, recruitment setting and region.
INTERPRETATION: The large, global dataset strengthens confidence in the elevated mental health burden among trans adults, though heterogeneity in assessment tools and recruitment settings limits precision. The absence of general-population comparators in most studies precludes direct risk ratio estimation; nonetheless, the absolute prevalences are markedly higher than general-population benchmarks. Funding sources were not reported, and selection bias cannot be ruled out in clinic-based samples.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the need for accessible, gender-affirming mental health services and routine screening for depression, suicidality and NSSI in trans adults, with particular attention to non-binary individuals and regional disparities.

item.title: Revisiting the link between childhood adversity and stress-sensitive brain regions in psychosis and bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated whether childhood adversity (CA) is associated with gray matter volume (GMV) reductions in stress-sensitive brain regions (hippocampus, amygdala, prefrontal cortex) in individuals with psychotic disorder (PD) or bipolar disorder (BD). The study synthesized findings from structural brain imaging studies to clarify inconsistent prior results.
FINDINGS: The review included 29 studies (n=3056; mean age 36.6±16.1; 47% female) of fair methodological quality with high heterogeneity. Most studies reported negative associations between CA and GMV, particularly in prefrontal regions. However, meta-analyses of 5 studies found no significant association between CA and hippocampal volume (p≥0.66), and 4 studies showed no association with amygdala volume (p≥0.87). Findings for the hippocampus and amygdala were largely null or inconsistent.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that CA is not consistently linked to hippocampal or amygdala volume reductions in PD/BD, despite many individual studies reporting negative associations. The stronger and more consistent pattern emerged in prefrontal regions, though high heterogeneity and fair study quality limit firm conclusions. The meta-analytic results are robust for the hippocampus and amygdala (no effect detected), but cortical findings remain preliminary and warrant cautious interpretation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a consistent neuroanatomical signature of CA in limbic structures among PD/BD patients. Clinicians should not assume hippocampal or amygdala atrophy is a direct consequence of CA in these populations. Further high-quality, longitudinal research is needed before considering structural brain changes as biomarkers of adversity in psychiatric care.

item.title: Estimating the Economic Value of Supported Online Parent-Led Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to Prevent Child Anxiety Problems: Economic Evaluation of the MYCATS Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the cost-effectiveness of a parent-led online supported cognitive behavioural therapy (OSI+TS) versus usual school practice (USP) for preventing anxiety in 4–7-year-olds identified by universal screening, using data from the MYCATS cluster RCT (n=865) with a 12-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: Children in the OSI+TS arm gained 0.021 (95 % CI 0.010–0.033) and 0.043 (95 % CI 0.021–0.064) QALYs under UK adult and Australia adolescent tariffs, respectively, at an extra cost of £244.16. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were £11 462 and £5 701 per QALY, with 88.2 % and 99.3 % probability of being cost-effective at the £20 000 threshold.
INTERPRETATION: The cluster-randomised design and prespecified economic analysis plan strengthen internal validity, and ICERs fall well below NICE thresholds. However, the absolute QALY gains are small and the perspective is limited to NHS/PSS costs; societal spill-over and long-term outcomes remain unexamined. The short 12-month horizon and reliance on tariff-based QALYs also limit interpretability for routine child psychiatry.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: OSI+TS appears economically attractive within current thresholds, but clinicians should note the modest health gains and the lack of evidence beyond one year; implementation should be monitored for real-world uptake and sustained benefit.

item.title: Initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly using a two-injection start in adult patients diagnosed with schizophrenia: real-world views and experiences of Italian healthcare professionals.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pan-European, non-interventional, cross-sectional online survey assessed Italian healthcare professionals' (HCPs) views and experiences regarding the two-injection start (TIS) initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg (AOM 400) in adult patients with schizophrenia, a method designed to simplify treatment initiation without prolonged oral supplementation.
FINDINGS: Responses from 108 Italian HCPs (47.2% of participants) showed that poor treatment adherence (81.5%), patient preference (50.0%), and disease relapse (42.6%) were common reasons for using AOM 400-TIS. Barriers included patient reluctance to receive two injections (36.1%), concerns about tolerability (24.1%), and safety concerns (23.1%). Most HCPs reported satisfactory patient outcomes (85.2%), ease of administration (82.4%), and a safety/tolerability profile similar to the traditional one-injection start (69.4%).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides descriptive insights into HCP perspectives but lacks comparative data or patient outcomes, limiting causal inferences. Selection bias may exist due to voluntary participation, and the cross-sectional design precludes assessment of long-term effects. While HCPs generally viewed AOM 400-TIS favorably, the absence of objective clinical metrics or patient-reported outcomes weakens the evidence. Further research is needed to validate these perceptions with clinical efficacy and safety data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests AOM 400-TIS is perceived as practical and well-tolerated by Italian HCPs, particularly for patients with adherence issues, but definitive clinical benefits remain unproven. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and tolerability concerns when choosing initiation methods, while awaiting more robust data.

item.title: Applying a Behavioral Fit Analysis with Sexual Minority Youth at Risk for Suicide.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review and conceptual paper addresses the elevated suicide risk among sexual minority (SM) youth (ages 15–24) and proposes a behavioral fit analysis framework to integrate minority stress and social drivers of health into suicide risk assessment and treatment planning. It synthesizes literature on minority stress and existing assessment tools, illustrating application via a fictional case example.
FINDINGS: The paper summarizes evidence that SM youth face disproportionate suicide risk due to minority stress and discrimination. It introduces a behavioral fit analysis to tailor evidence-based suicide interventions by incorporating social determinants linked to SM identity. A fictional case demonstrates how this framework guides individualized treatment planning.
INTERPRETATION: This is a narrative review with illustrative case material, not empirical research. It offers a conceptual model rather than quantitative outcomes, so no effect sizes, p-values, or confidence intervals are reported. The strength lies in highlighting the relevance of social drivers of health in suicide prevention for SM youth, but the lack of empirical validation and reliance on a single fictional example limit internal validity and generalizability. External validity is uncertain as the framework has not been tested in real-world clinical settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The proposed behavioral fit analysis may help clinicians consider minority stress and social context when assessing and treating suicidal SM youth, but it should be viewed as a preliminary framework. Clinicians should await empirical evaluation before adopting it as standard practice.

item.title: Development and preliminary evaluation of a group adaptation of the Unified Protocol for Transdiagnostic Treatment of Emotional Disorders in adolescents (UP-A) in a Spanish public mental health center.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study adapted the Unified Protocol for Transdiagnostic Treatment of Emotional Disorders in Adolescents (UP-A) into a group format and evaluated its feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness in a Spanish public outpatient mental health setting. This open-label, single-arm pilot study included 31 adolescents (mean age 14.03; 87.1% female).
FINDINGS: 80.65% of participants completed the 16-session group intervention. High satisfaction and therapeutic alliance were reported by adolescents and parents. Significant improvements were observed in adolescent-reported emotional symptoms (effect size not reported) and emotion regulation strategies, alongside parent-reported reductions in depressive symptoms. Clinician ratings showed reduced diagnostic severity and improved functioning.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to the single-arm design, lack of a control group, small sample size, and retrospective trial registration, which raises concerns about selection bias and confounding. While the high completion rate and positive outcomes suggest feasibility and acceptability, the absence of randomization and blinding limits internal validity. The lack of effect sizes and confidence intervals precludes assessment of clinical significance. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The results suggest potential for group-based UP-A in public mental health settings, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend routine adoption. Clinicians should await confirmatory trials before considering this approach over established treatments.

item.title: The utility of animal models in hiPSC-based studies of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a common and heritable neurodevelopmental condition. This systematic review (PRISMA-guided) examined how often animal models or animal-derived cells are still used alongside human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) research in ASD, questioning whether such animal use is necessary.
FINDINGS: Out of 207 hiPSC-based ASD studies (2009–2024), 79 (38.16%) also involved animals or animal-derived cells. Nearly half used animal models to study ASD neurobiology, while others employed animals for unrelated purposes (e.g., teratoma assays to confirm pluripotency or extracting primary astrocytes for co-culture, which may introduce confounding variables).
INTERPRETATION: The review suggests that animal use in hiPSC-based ASD research is frequent and sometimes unnecessary, potentially undermining the ethical and translational rationale for reducing animal experiments. However, the study does not assess the scientific contribution of animal components or whether their exclusion would compromise study validity. The review is limited by its descriptive nature and lack of critical appraisal of individual study designs or outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For clinicians, this review highlights a gap between the ethical goal of reducing animal use in ASD research and current practices. It does not directly inform patient care but underscores the need for clearer justification when animals are included in hiPSC-based studies.

item.title: Working with goals in youth mental health and substance use service: A review of current practice guidelines and recommendations.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines practice guidelines and recommendations for working with goals in youth mental health and substance use services (ages 10–25), focusing on therapeutic relationships, shared decision-making, and equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI). It synthesizes academic and clinical guidebooks published between 2003 and 2023 to assess how current practices embed EDI and cultural safety.
FINDINGS: The review identified 53 publications and distilled four themes: (1) semi-structured goal-setting with routine outcome monitoring; (2) youth- and family-centered engagement strategies; (3) conceptual integration of goals within therapy; and (4) a growing but still limited emphasis on EDI and cultural safety. No quantitative outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study provides a qualitative synthesis rather than empirical evidence. Strengths include broad coverage of guidelines and explicit attention to equity, but limitations include lack of systematic quality assessment, absence of quantitative data, and potential selection bias in included sources. The clinical recommendations remain conceptual, with uncertain generalizability and no direct evidence of improved outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the review supports adopting collaborative, youth-informed goal-setting practices, it does not provide measurable benefits or validated frameworks. Clinicians may consider integrating routine outcome monitoring and EDI principles, but should await empirical validation of these approaches before expecting measurable improvements in youth mental health outcomes.

item.title: Abnormalities of intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression: a meta-analysis of resting-state functional imaging studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined resting-state functional neuroimaging studies to identify consistent abnormalities in intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression (LLD) compared with healthy controls (HC). The clinical question was whether reproducible neural signatures exist that could clarify neuropathology and potentially aid diagnosis or treatment development.
FINDINGS: Thirteen studies (476 LLD patients vs 394 HC) were meta-analysed using anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping. Higher activity in LLD was found in the left fusiform gyrus (FG), right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) and right middle frontal gyrus (MFG), while lower activity was observed in the left supplementary motor area (SMA), left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and left postcentral gyrus (PoCG). Subgroup analyses by functional index and statistical correction showed largely consistent patterns, with additional involvement of the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG) in corrected analyses.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but methodologically heterogeneous (varied imaging indices, correction methods, and small samples). The use of anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping improves robustness, yet the findings remain correlational and cannot establish causality. The reported regions are plausible but effect sizes are not quantified numerically in the abstract, limiting assessment of clinical significance. External validity is uncertain because included studies may overrepresent specific LLD subgroups and settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest potential neural correlates of LLD that could inform future diagnostic or therapeutic targeting, but they do not yet support changes in routine clinical practice. Clinicians should await larger, longitudinal studies with harmonised imaging protocols before considering any neuroimaging-based interventions.

item.title: Neural mechanisms of guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a protocol for a prospective multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aims to investigate the neural mechanisms of guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (ICBT) in children with ADHD using multimodal MRI, addressing a gap in understanding how ICBT affects brain structure and function. It is a protocol for a prospective study embedded within an ongoing randomized, sham-controlled ICBT trial, involving approximately 60 children with ADHD and typically developing (TD) controls for baseline comparisons.
FINDINGS: The study will compare pre- and post-intervention MRI scans (structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion tensor imaging) in children with ADHD randomized to ICBT or sham control. Baseline MRI data from TD children will serve as a reference. Analyses will focus on intervention-related neural changes and associations between baseline MRI markers and clinical treatment response.
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, this study has not yet produced results, so no findings or effect sizes are available. The design is strong in its randomized, sham-controlled framework and multimodal MRI approach, which could provide valuable mechanistic insights. However, external validity will depend on the representativeness of the sample and the clinical setting. The study’s novelty lies in exploring neural predictors of treatment response, but results are pending.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This research could eventually identify neural biomarkers predicting ICBT response in children with ADHD, potentially personalizing treatment. However, until results are published, no clinical changes should be made based on this protocol alone.

item.title: Aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare complication of clozapine treatment ‒ a case of a patient with paranoid schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a single case report describing a 54-year-old woman with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia who developed aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare adverse effect of clozapine therapy. The report highlights an atypical and previously undocumented complication of clozapine.
FINDINGS: The patient developed inflammatory changes in the aorta (aortitis) accompanied by eosinophilia while on clozapine. Symptoms resolved after discontinuation of the medication. No quantitative data (e.g., laboratory values, imaging metrics, or follow-up duration) are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is extremely limited (a single case report) and lacks generalizability. There are no comparative data, effect sizes, or statistical analyses. The causal relationship between clozapine and aortitis is plausible but unproven in this context. The report serves primarily to raise awareness of a potential rare adverse effect rather than to establish causality or guide treatment decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case suggests that clinicians should consider clozapine-induced aortitis in patients on clozapine who present with eosinophilia and unexplained vascular symptoms. However, given the rarity and lack of prior reports, routine screening for aortitis in asymptomatic patients on clozapine is not justified based on this evidence alone. Further investigation is needed before any practice change.

item.title: Treatment Fidelity of AquOTic: An Occupational Therapy-Based Aquatic Intervention for Children on the Autism Spectrum.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the treatment fidelity of AquOTic, a manualized 10-week occupational therapy-based aquatic intervention for autistic children (aged 5–9 years), using a descriptive design nested within a larger RCT. The goal was to evaluate whether core therapeutic components were delivered consistently to support reproducibility and water-safety outcomes.
FINDINGS: Mean adherence by swim buddies was 95.93%. Component-level fidelity averaged 97.36%, and core ingredients (play-based strategies, modeling, water-property integration) were present in 100% of analyzed sessions (N = 37 children; N = 18 swim buddies).
INTERPRETATION: The high fidelity scores strengthen internal validity by confirming that the intervention was delivered as intended. However, the descriptive design lacks a comparator and does not link fidelity to clinical outcomes (e.g., drowning risk reduction). External validity is limited to a single county therapy pool and trained graduate students, so generalizability to routine pediatric OT settings remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results suggest AquOTic can be implemented with high fidelity in controlled settings, supporting its potential for replication. Clinicians should note that fidelity alone does not guarantee improved water safety; effectiveness trials are still needed.

item.title: Psychosocial Interventions for Sexual and Gender Minority Youth with Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Suicide is a leading cause of death among U.S. adolescents, with sexual and gender minority youth (SGMY) facing disproportionately higher risks. This scoping review examined randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of psychosocial interventions targeting suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) in LGBTQIA+ adolescents, aiming to map the evidence base and identify gaps.
FINDINGS: A systematic search (2013–2025) identified 23 unique RCTs: 6 with published results, 8 protocols, and 9 trial registrations. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and family-based therapy were the most common modalities, with over half incorporating online components (e.g., virtual sessions or apps). No pooled effect sizes or comparative outcomes were reported due to heterogeneity and limited published data.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely sparse—only 6 completed RCTs over 11 years—despite SGMY’s elevated suicide risk. The review highlights methodological diversity (e.g., modalities, delivery formats) but lacks quantitative synthesis or clear efficacy data. Funding sources and risk of bias were not assessed in the abstract, limiting conclusions about internal validity. The findings underscore a critical gap: RCTs tailored to SGMY’s unique needs are urgently needed before any treatment recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice cannot rely on RCT evidence for psychosocial interventions targeting STBs in SGMY. Clinicians should prioritize established suicide prevention strategies (e.g., CBT for general adolescent populations) while advocating for research to address this high-risk group’s specific needs.

item.title: Changes in opioid prescribing and high-risk co-prescribing after implementation of the 2016 CDC opioid guideline among older adults with and without cancer.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined how the 2016 CDC opioid prescribing guideline affected opioid prescribing patterns and high-risk co-prescribing (with benzodiazepines, antidepressants, or sedatives) among older adults with and without cancer, using SEER-Medicare data (2014–2017). This retrospective cohort study assessed changes in opioid use before and after guideline implementation.
FINDINGS: The study included 42,931 cancer patients and 108,218 non-cancer patients. After guideline implementation, opioid prescribing declined in both groups, but reductions were larger in non-cancer patients. Difference-in-difference estimates showed smaller reductions among cancer patients in monthly opioid prescribing (-0.14; 95% CI, -0.17 to -0.11; p < 0.0001) and days of supply (-3.07; 95% CI, -3.68 to -2.45; p < 0.0001). Changes in daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) were not significant (16.73; 95% CI, -43.36 to 76.82; p = 0.5853). High-risk co-prescribing declined overall but decreased less among cancer patients for all combinations (all p < 0.0001).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-quality evidence from a large, well-defined cohort with robust statistical adjustment. However, the observational design cannot establish causality, and residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured clinical factors) may persist. The clinical significance of the observed differences is uncertain, as effect sizes were modest and MME changes were not significant. The findings suggest guideline adherence was stronger in non-cancer patients, possibly due to differing pain management needs or perceived risks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The results highlight potential gaps in opioid prescribing practices among older adults with cancer post-guideline implementation. Clinicians should remain vigilant about balancing pain control and safety, particularly in cancer patients where reductions in high-risk co-prescribing were less pronounced. Further research is needed to determine optimal prescribing strategies in this population.

item.title: A healthier day, a healthier mind: linking 24-h movement behavior guideline adherence to mental health in university students.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study in Chinese university students (n=1,856) examined whether adherence to 24-hour movement behavior guidelines (physical activity, screen time, sleep) is associated with positive mental health, and whether university adaptation and psychological resilience mediate this relationship.
FINDINGS: Adherence to all three guidelines was low, with sleep duration highest and screen time lowest. Greater adherence correlated modestly with better mental health (r = 0.286–0.318), university adaptation, and resilience. Serial mediation analysis suggested indirect effects of guideline adherence on mental health via adaptation and resilience, but effect sizes were not reported.
INTERPRETATION: The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The modest correlations and lack of effect sizes limit clinical interpretation. While the proposed mediation pathways are plausible, the study cannot confirm whether improving movement behaviors would enhance mental health or adaptation. Funding sources and potential confounders (e.g., socioeconomic status, baseline mental health) were not addressed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice. Encouraging movement behaviors may support mental health indirectly, but high-quality longitudinal or interventional studies are needed to test causality and quantify meaningful effects.

item.title: Sleep disturbances and functional impairment in severe mental illness: A structural equation modeling study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study investigated how sleep disturbances relate to functional impairment in outpatients with severe mental illness (SMI), using structural equation modeling to disentangle direct and indirect pathways via psychiatric symptoms.
FINDINGS: Among 229 SMI outpatients, 69 % screened positive for at least one sleep disturbance; poor sleep quality was reported by 55.5 % and high OSA risk by 45.8 %. In the SEM, depressive/anxious symptoms (β = 0.45), negative symptoms (β = 0.38), manic symptoms (β = 0.17), and OSA risk (β = 0.41) were independently associated with functional impairment. Insomnia showed a paradoxical pattern: a direct negative effect (β = –0.47) but an indirect positive effect via depressive/anxious symptoms (β = 0.22).
INTERPRETATION: The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, precluding causal inference. SEM provides a nuanced view, but reliance on screening questionnaires rather than objective sleep measures and the single-site recruitment may reduce generalisability. The effect sizes suggest that depressive/anxious symptoms and OSA risk are the most robust correlates of functional impairment, whereas insomnia’s dual pathways warrant further longitudinal investigation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for sleep disturbances—especially OSA risk and mood/anxiety symptoms—may help identify modifiable targets to improve functioning in SMI, but treatment trials are needed to confirm whether intervening on these factors changes functional outcomes.

item.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Risk of Kidney Replacement Therapy and Health Care Utilization in Bipolar Disorder With Chronic Kidney Disease.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This real-world cohort study used TriNetX data to test whether GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reduce the need for kidney replacement therapy (KRT) and health care utilisation (HCU) versus active comparators in adults with bipolar disorder (BD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD stage ≤3). The primary comparison was GLP-1 RA versus DPP-4 inhibitors; a secondary comparison was versus RAAS inhibitors.
FINDINGS: After propensity-score matching (n=3,908 per group), GLP-1 RA use was associated with a lower risk of KRT (aHR 0.56, 95% CI 0.50–0.64) and lower HCU (aHR 0.74, 95% CI 0.71–0.78) versus DPP-4 inhibitors. Five-year KRT-free survival was 87.93% vs 84.63% (P<.001). In the secondary analysis (n=2,539 per group), GLP-1 RA vs RAAS inhibitors also showed lower KRT risk (aHR 0.66) and HCU (aHR 0.62), with KRT-free survival 94.68% vs 89.77% (P<.001). Benefits were consistent across sex, race, obesity, and psychotropic subgroups, including lithium users.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s large real-world cohorts and active-comparator design strengthen internal validity, but residual confounding and non-randomised treatment assignment remain concerns. The magnitude of KRT reduction (absolute gain ~3–5% at 5 years) is clinically modest. HCU differences were not consistently significant across comparators, suggesting possible outcome-reporting or care-pattern artefacts. The findings are exploratory and require prospective randomised evidence to confirm causality and generalisability to routine BD+CKD care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data suggest GLP-1 RA may offer kidney protection in BD+CKD, but the effect size is modest and not yet definitive. Consider GLP-1 RA in BD patients with CKD for potential renal benefits, while awaiting confirmatory trials; monitor kidney function and glycaemic control closely.

item.title: Functioning Management & Recovery - Resource Group, a psychoeducational intervention to improve empowerment of people with severe mental illness: a 12-month multicenter randomized control study.
item.description: AIM: Functioning Management and Recovery with the Resource Group (FM&R-GR) is a standardized Psychoeducational Intervention elaborated to improve functioning and empowerment of people with Severe Mental Illness (SMI) living in the community. The aim of this study is to prove its efficacy by the primary and secondary outcomes. METHODS: 60 patients with SMI were recruited in 5 day-centers (North and South Italy) randomly assigned into 2 groups (Experimental vs Control); patients underwent a multicenter follow-up study with a two time-point evaluation (t0, pre-treatment and t1, 12 months).

item.title: Brief internet intervention for grieving children and adolescents: co-design and trial protocol.
item.description: Background: Internet interventions may improve access to help for grieving young people. In feedback from recent trials of internet interventions for grief, youth emphasised treatments should be shorter to address lack of time, which was the main barrier to uptake.Objective: The aim was to co-design a new brief internet intervention for grieving children and adolescents, and to outline a protocol for a pilot feasibility randomised controlled trial.Method: Nine children and adolescents (mean age = 15.22, 77.7% female, 33.3% male) co-designed the brief internet intervention.Results: A randomised […]

item.title: To Relax or Not to Relax for Anxious Youth? Findings from a Survey of Exposure Specialists.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Relaxation is a commonly used, albeit controversial, therapy technique to support anxious youth. Increasingly, clinical trial data suggest little added benefit, and potentially a contraindication, for the use of relaxation strategies for pediatric anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders above and beyond that of exposure therapy. However, many clinicians, even those with substantial experience delivering exposure therapy, will at times incorporate relaxation into their treatment. How and when it is best to do so remains poorly articulated in the clinical trial literature.

item.title: Investigating Potential Adverse Drug Reactions of Lisdexamfetamine Using Sequence Symmetry Analysis.
item.description: The prevalence of ADHD is increasing rapidly, and lisdexamfetamine is increasingly popular, but few studies investigate its safety. We performed a sequence symmetry analysis (SSA) using Danish register data to identify potential ADRs associated with lisdexamfetamine in 2013-2023. Outcomes were incident prescriptions or incident discharge diagnoses. We calculated trend-adjusted sequence ratios (SR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).

item.title: An Effective Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection Framework Using Adaptive Serial Hybrid Network With Self-Calibrated Feature Extraction on Brain MRI Images.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a medical condition commonly categorized as a neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients with ASD are not limited to common symptoms, and it often requires long-term hospital visits and specialists for definitive evaluation. Research has highlighted the importance of early intervention and care for ASD patients, as it can benefit their lifestyle.

item.title: Effects of early-life tactile experience enrichment on autistic-like behaviors and synaptic alterations in Shank3 mutant mice.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to limited treatment options. While non-pharmacological approaches based on sensory stimulation have shown promise in clinical practice, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study explored the therapeutic potential of tactile experience enrichment (TEE) during specific developmental windows in Shank3 KO mice, a model of ASD.

item.title: Enhanced Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Adolescents: Impacts of Individualized Skills Coaching on Constructs of Suicidality.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Suicide is a leading cause of death and significant concerns for adolescents and young adults. Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Adolescents (DBT-A) is an evidence-based intervention that effectively reduces life-threatening behaviors. Limited research examines the impact of adding individualized skills coaching sessions (ISCS) to the DBT-A model, a novel intervention referred to in this paper as "Enhanced DBT-A." This study evaluates the effectiveness of Enhanced DBT-A in reducing suicidality over 1 year of treatment in an outpatient and intensive outpatient setting.

item.title: Effectiveness of Outpatient Adolescent Dialectical Behavior Therapy Adapted for Spanish-Speaking Families: A Retrospective Chart Review.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Latinx adolescents are the largest minoritized ethnic group in the United States. They are at elevated risk for suicidal and non-suicidal behaviors and symptoms of borderline personality disorder (BPD). Dialectical behavior therapy for adolescents (DBT-A) is an evidence-based treatment that targets these behaviors, yet limited evidence exists on the effectiveness of adapting DBT-A to Latinx adolescents with Spanish-speaking families.

item.title: Patient experiences of benzodiazepine tapering: a qualitative study of treatment in addiction care.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Tapering by gradual dose reduction is a key component of treatment for individuals with addiction to benzodiazepines. Although many patients recover, treatment dropouts and relapses are common. Few studies have explored how benzodiazepine tapering is experienced from the patient perspective. METHODS: This qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with 19 adults with addiction to benzodiazepines who were undergoing tapering treatment at a publicly funded outpatient addiction clinic. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyze the data.

item.title: Unraveling the multifaceted relationship between creativity and mental health with longitudinal analyses of genotyped twins.
item.description: Existing findings of creativity and mental health associations are inconsistent, partly due to heterogeneous assessment of creativity and mental health. Consequently, basic questions concerning the direction and domain specificity of these associations remain unanswered. This comprehensive study used data from 14 658 Swedish twins, including a genotyped subsample, and employed a range of genetically informed and longitudinal designs to examine the direction, nature, and underlying mechanisms of the creativity-mental health relationship.

item.title: Real-world alcohol cue exposure and drinking risk in alcohol use disorder.
item.description: Alcohol-related cues are thought to contribute to drinking in alcohol use disorder (AUD), but their contribution in daily life remains difficult to separate from changing social contexts and internal states.

item.title: Re-examining externalizing polygenic risks and psychosocial environments: Are gene-environment correlations really that pervasive?
item.description: BACKGROUND: Gene-environment correlations (rGEs) are often observed for psychiatric traits, including externalizing problems. Some researchers believe rGEs reflect the effects of offspring genotype on psychosocial environments. Others consider rGEs to be a nuisance, reflecting effects of confounders, such as population stratification, assortative mating, or parental genotypes. Our study aims to examine whether rGEs persist when confounding effects are controlled for in a family-based design.

item.title: Treatment Patterns and Clinical Outcomes in Youth With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: The co-occurrence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is common and associated with greater clinical complexity. This study evaluated real-world treatment patterns and outcomes among children and adolescents with ADHD, comparing those with and without comorbid ASD. METHOD: A retrospective comparative cohort study analyzed electronic health records from the TriNetX Research Network, including 869,510 children and adolescents aged 3 to 18 years with ADHD, of whom 155,543 (17.9%) had ASD.

item.title: Clinicians' Impressions of the Developmental Appropriateness of the Ask-Suicide Screening Questions for Children Aged 6-12.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Although the suicide rate for children ages 8-12 is increasing, there is not a developmentally adapted suicide risk screener for children younger than 10. Current practices to screen preteen children for suicide risk often include unstructured interviewing and/or suicide risk screeners that are validated for use with older children. It is clinically important to understand the limitations of existing suicide risk screeners when they are used with preteens to inform the design of developmentally appropriate measures and to tailor support for clinicians.

item.title: Contraceptive use in women of childbearing age with bipolar disorder.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Unplanned pregnancies are frequent in women with bipolar disorder (BD) while perinatal period is associated with a higher risk of relapse. Effective contraception during childbearing age in BD could reduce the risk of unplanned pregnancy and its consequences. The present study studied the prevalence of contraceptive use and which sociodemographic and clinical variables affect its use in women with BD. METHODS: 796 women (18-50 years old) with BD were recruited and evaluated by the MONTRA survey in France among hospital and consultant psychiatrists.

item.title: [Differential diagnosis between Bipolar Disorder and behavioral variant Frontotemporal Dementia: the role of longitudinal neuropsychological assessment. A Case Report.].
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Bipolar Disorder (BD) and the behavioral variant of Frontotemporal Dementia (bvFTD) can present overlapping clinical features in their early stages, characterized by disinhibition, euphoria, and executive function deficits. Differential diagnosis is particularly challenging when behavioral symptoms are accompanied by evidence of cortical atrophy on neuroimaging. CASE PRESENTATION: We describe the case of a 48-year-old woman diagnosed with Type I BD since age 25, referred for suspected bvFTD due to a progressive decline in memory functions and sleep disturbances.

item.title: Treating PTSD in a cognitive-behavioural paradigm.
item.description: Significant advances have been made over the past two decades, associated with an increase in methodologically advanced research, into the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, interest in the topic of PTSD has not only not waned, but seems to be gaining strength. The main reason for this is the difficulty in clearly defining the phenomenon, which is related to the constant updating of the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder in medical classifications.

item.title: Toward Scalable Driver Readiness Screenings for Autistic Teens: Clinical Measures Correlated With Real-World Evaluations.
item.description: ImportanceThere are no standardized pathways to guide autistic adolescents through the learning-to-drive process, beginning with deciding whether they are ready to pursue driving.ObjectiveTo examine whether commonly used clinical assessments correlate with driver readiness determinations.DesignCross-sectional, nonexperimental study using a single in-person visit comprised of a clinical assessment and on-road passenger activities.SettingA primary care clinic in an urban city.ParticipantsTwenty-one autistic adolescents aged 15-19 years without a learner's permit were recruited via email outreach […]

item.title: Maternal Diet and Offspring ASD and ADHD: A Critical Narrative Review of Dietary Patterns, Choline, and Polyphenol-Related Exposures.
item.description: Maternal diet may influence fetal neurodevelopment through nutrient availability, placental function, and maternal-fetal metabolite signaling. This critical narrative review used a structured, purposive search to organize human evidence on prenatal dietary patterns, choline, and polyphenol-related exposures according to outcome directness: diagnosed autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), related dimensional traits, and general neurodevelopment.

item.title: Cerebral Lateralization for Language as a Potential Biomarker for the Broad Autism Phenotype: A Functional Transcranial Doppler Ultrasonography Investigation.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with language deficits, while growing evidence suggests that atypical cerebral lateralization for language could serve as a potential neural marker for ASD. The present study seeks to investigate cerebral lateralization for language not only in terms of ASD, but also as a potential biomarker for the broad autism phenotype (BAP)-a sum of subclinical traits similar to those of ASD.

item.title: Real-World Functional Gains in Thai Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A 24-Month Naturalistic Study.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the 24-month longitudinal trajectories of symptom severity and functional impairment in children diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). METHODS: This longitudinal observational study recruited newly diagnosed children aged 6-12 years from a child and adolescent outpatient clinic.

item.title: When should a clinician stop trying to prevent a patient's suicide? Commentary on Campione and Joiner (2026).
item.description: Comments on the article by M. Campione and T. Joiner (see record 2027-58493-001), which highlights the alarmingly high rate of use of Canada's medical assistance in dying program. Campione and Joiner clearly and cogently describe how the structure of this program may allow clinicians to hasten the death of people who are not terminally ill and who instead have untreated psychopathology. They articulate significant concerns with the medical assistance in dying program in its current form.

item.title: SOS for School Staff Suicide Prevention Program: Perspectives of School Staff.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Schools play an important role in child and adolescent suicide prevention efforts and many states have begun to mandate suicide prevention education for school staff. OBJECTIVE: This study explored school staff's (N = 1509) perceptions of the impact of a brief virtual suicide prevention course titled: SOS for School Staff. METHOD: This study used an online posttest and three-month follow-up to explore school staff's (N = 1509) perceptions via a posttest and follow-up measuring preparation, confidence, and knowledge.

item.title: Clinician Recommendations for the Assessment of Preteen Suicide Risk: A Qualitative Study.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: To better understand clinician practices for assessing preteen suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) as an initial step to inform the development of a comprehensive suicide risk assessment for this age group. METHOD: We conducted qualitative interviews with child mental health clinicians (N = 31) who routinely assess preteens and clinical researchers with expertise in child and adolescent suicide. item.title: High Anemia Awareness Does Not Mitigate Insomnia Risk in Ghanaian University Students: A Cross-Sectional Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Anemia and insomnia represent significant public health concerns among university students. However, their interrelationship and the potential role of anemia prevention knowledge in mitigating these conditions remain unexplored in Ghanaian tertiary institutions. AIM: This study determined the prevalence of anemia and insomnia among Ghanaian university students. Likewise, the knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding anemia prevention and the association between anemia prevention knowledge and insomnia status were explored.

item.title: Development and validation of the Beliefs in Social Anxiety Scale (BIAS) for Chinese socially anxious adults and adolescents.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Maladaptive social beliefs play a pivotal role in the development and maintenance of social anxiety; however, existing measures have limited cultural adaptability for Chinese populations. Therefore, this study developed and validated the Beliefs in Social Anxiety Scale (BIAS), designed to assess maladaptive social beliefs among Chinese adolescents and adults. METHODS: Three studies were conducted to examine its psychometric properties using data from community samples of Chinese adolescents and adults. Study 1 employed a mixed-methods approach.

item.title: The role of plasma oxytocin in early-onset schizophrenia: implications for disease severity and early intervention.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Early-onset schizophrenia (EOS) is a severe psychiatric disorder with poor long-term outcomes. It offers a unique opportunity to examine the neurobiological mechanisms of schizophrenia without the confounding effects of adult environmental factors. Oxytocin (OXT), a neuropeptide involved in social and emotional regulation, has been linked to several psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia. This study investigated associations between plasma OXT levels, disease severity, personality traits, and childhood trauma in EOS.

item.title: Letting patients lead? Practitioners' experiences of using DIALOG+ in psychosis outpatient care - patient involvement, collaborative dynamics, and professional roles.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Severe mental illness, such as psychosis, significantly affects many areas of life. Involving patients in their care may enhance engagement and support recovery by ensuring that treatment focuses on their expressed needs. DIALOG+ is an intervention, supported by a digital tool, aimed at facilitating patient involvement in treatment by incorporating self-assessment and a problem-solving approach during routine clinical encounters and promoting a collaborative and patient-centred approach to care.

item.title: Energy landscape and dynamic state modeling for schizophrenia biomarker extraction in task-based fMRI.
item.description: Task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) examines how the brain dynamically responds to cognitive and perceptual demands, offering complementary insight beyond traditional activation-based analyses in schizophrenia. Prior task-based fMRI studies have identified reduced functional connectivity within auditory and associated cortical areas.

item.title: Neurobiological etiology of impulsivity in the context of aggressive behaviors in schizophrenia.
item.description: The main aim of the article was to show the importance of impulsivity as a background to aggressive behaviour displayed by people on the schizophrenia spectrum with particular attention to its biological determinants, including genetic ones. Imaging tests of the central nervous system allow for locating the centres responsible for particular types of impulsiveness and for modulating impulsive reactions.
